stem: Hand-wiring dependencies (new A(new B(new C()))) becomes the maintenance burden because:
options: Every added constructor parameter RIPPLES through every place that builds the object - and real apps have hundreds
explanation: The wiring itself is what a container solves - and the ONLY thing. At small scale, hand-wiring is correct (2.13).

stem: provider.GetRequiredService<ReportService>() builds the whole object graph by:
options: Reading the constructor via reflection (4.11), supplying each dependency and THEIRS recursively
explanation: Register the recipe once; the container assembles the graph. Add a fifth parameter tomorrow and nothing else changes.

stem: AddSingleton means the container hands out:
options: ONE instance for the whole application - config, caches
explanation: The lesson's counter shows #1 every time, across scopes. A singleton must be THREAD-SAFE - every request shares it (6.1).

options: ONE per scope - the same within a scope, a new one in the next (in ASP.NET a scope IS a request)
explanation: The counter: #1 twice in scope 1, #2 in scope 2. Per-request state lives here.

options: A NEW instance every time it is resolved - the safe default for cheap, stateless services
explanation: The counter shows #1 then #2 within one scope. Transient is the default; scoped and singleton are deliberate choices.

stem: The composition root principle says registration happens:
options: In ONE place at startup - everywhere else, classes just declare constructor parameters
explanation: Nobody else calls new or touches the container. Dependencies stay visible in constructor signatures.

stem: Injecting the ServiceProvider itself and calling GetService inside classes is:
options: The SERVICE LOCATOR anti-pattern - it HIDES dependencies again, undoing what constructor injection fixed
explanation: A dependency belongs in the signature, visible. Asking the container for it from inside buries it once more.

stem: new ReportService(new FakeOrderStore(), ...) in a test shows that:
options: DI the PRINCIPLE makes testing possible; the CONTAINER is only scale convenience - tests pass fakes directly
explanation: The 2.13 RecordingSender move: no SQL, no SMTP, no container. Unit tests usually skip the container entirely.

stem: A DI container is overkill for:
options: A console tool with five classes - new them up in Main and be done (as this course does)
explanation: The principle always; the container when the wiring HURTS. ASP.NET is built on this exact container, so AddSingleton there IS this lesson.

stem: A SCOPED service captured by a SINGLETON is a bug because:
options: The scoped object OUTLIVES its scope - held by the app-lifetime singleton, causing subtle corruption
explanation: The singleton pins one scoped instance forever, defeating per-request isolation. Lifetime mismatches are the classic DI trap.
